title: Navigating the What Happened Conversation
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece dissects the common leadership ritual of the 'What Happened?' conversation that follows a mistake, arguing that its typical framing inadvertently puts team members on the defensive. The author identifies the frustrated tone and the word 'So' as tells of a blame-oriented version of this conversation, and contrasts it with a learning-oriented alternative built around different questions. This shift changes the relationship dynamics entirely. The piece closes by asserting that the trust built through a learning-focused response is worth more than any short-term catharsis.
points: The default 'What Happened?' framing puts team members on the defensive by implicitly treating them as guilty until proven innocent.
Replacing 'What Happened?' with learning-oriented questions shifts the conversation from blame to practical problem-solving.
Team members who feel supported rather than accused during a mistake-related conversation develop a tighter bond with that leader.
The piece explicitly argues the relational value of a learning-focused response outweighs any catharsis from venting frustration.
quotes: A frustrated leader typically starts the What Happened? conversation with a tone of disbelief, impatience, or uncomfortable surprise. The word “So” normally precedes the question, pointing to an obvious or avoidable mistake.
By requiring that they explain themselves, leaders inadvertently suggest the other party is guilty until proven innocent.
With the focus on learning and not blame, those on the receiving end feel supported, not accused.
Confronted by questions with a learning focus, team members drop their defensiveness and get highly practical about the insights worth acting on in the future.
The value of that connection is worth far more than any catharsis gained by frustration. Once again, when it comes to leadership, learning trumps blame.
